sceneHappening: Jesus is greater than Moses, and the wilderness generation is a warning not to harden our hearts
summary: "Therefore, holy brothers, partakers of a heavenly calling, consider the Apostle and High Priest of our confession: Jesus, who was faithful to him who appointed him, as also Moses was in all his house. For he has been counted worthy of more glory than Moses, because he who built the house has more honor than the house." "Moses indeed was faithful in all his house as a servant... but Christ is faithful as a Son over his house. We are his house, if we hold fast our confidence and the glorying of our hope firm to the end." Then Psalm 95 is quoted at length: "Today if you will hear his voice, don't harden your hearts, as in the rebellion, like as in the day of the trial in the wilderness, where your fathers tested me and tried me, and saw my deeds for forty years... As I swore in my wrath, 'They will not enter into my rest.'" "Beware, brothers, lest perhaps there might be in any one of you an evil heart of unbelief, in falling away from the living God; but exhort one another day by day, so long as it is called 'today', lest any one of you be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin. For we have become partakers of Christ, if we hold the beginning of our confidence firm to the end." The wilderness generation: "all those who came out of Egypt led by Moses... those who sinned, whose bodies fell in the wilderness... those who were disobedient... weren't able to enter in because of unbelief."
whySettingMatters: Comparing Jesus with Moses is a natural next step for readers with a Jewish background, since Moses was the greatest figure in their story and the giver of the law. The letter does not belittle Moses; it affirms his faithfulness and then shows that the builder is greater than the house and a son greater than a servant. Verse 6, "we are his house, if we hold fast," is the first of several "if" statements in Hebrews that tie belonging to endurance (3:14; 6:4-6; 10:26-31). How these "if" statements fit with assurance has been debated: some read them as warnings that real believers need to heed to persevere, some as warnings that apply to people who only appear to be believers, and some as describing a real loss of reward or of blessing. The long quotation from Psalm 95 sets up the reading of the next chapter. The wilderness generation is the example of a group that was saved from Egypt yet died in the desert, and the point is that rescue in the past does not guarantee entry into rest in the future. "Forty years" in the psalm is set against the "forty years" of the wilderness, and "today" is read as an open door that remains until the end of the age.

people.note: The Apostle and High Priest of our confession, faithful over God's house as a Son.
Faithful in all God's house as a servant.
Told they are God's house "if" they hold fast.

questions: Moses is honored but Jesus is greater. How does the letter honor the old while showing the new?
"Today if you will hear his voice, don't harden your hearts." What does it mean to harden a heart, and how does it happen slowly?
"Exhort one another day by day." What would a community that did that look like?
The "if" in verses 6 and 14 sits beside the confidence that God keeps his people. How do you hold both?
